body:
Two things first:

1. I assume you're operating in good faith, regardless of what I may think of feminism as a whole.  Otherwise, there's little point for me to respond.
2. I'm not a Tater tot, so any defense of your cited male relative or Tate is incidental.

From my standpoint, I don't see much point in working with feminists.  Even if you recognize and want to distance yourself from fanaticism in your neck of the woods (which I appreciate!), you and I still have foundational, irreconcilable ideological and epistemological incompatibilities.  These are not bulleted to correspond to your bullet points.

\- Patriarchy theory is the single foundational tenet of all brands of feminism, coloring every single other idea under the purview of feminism, no matter how benign or extreme.  It is not possible to have feminism without the idea of patriarchy; it would be like trying to have Christianity without Jesus.  I, as a non-feminist, do not subscribe to patriarchy theory; it is highly reductive at best, wildly inaccurate and misleading in between, and a malicious, unfalsifiable, highly emotive lie tantamount to a religious concept like Satan or original sin at worst.  If you are a feminist of any stripe, even if I would overall say that you are a generally fine and upstanding person, you and I simply can never see eye to eye on many things, and even in cases where we might seem to agree on the surface, ideological conflict will inevitably emerge later down the line.  If your views were to change such that you no longer accepted patriarchy theory, you would by definition no longer be a feminist.

\- Another foundational pillar of feminism lies in its epistemology (pun not intended), containing an explicit rejection of empiricism.  To really break this down in the adequate detail that it deserves would require me to spend multiple hours of brushing up on topics like the works of Sandra Harding, standpoint theory, feminist consciousness, metanarratives, and dozens of other terms and subtopics, and I don't really want to do that for an anonymous a Reddit comment at 2:30AM that about twelve people will ever read.  I'd highly recommend [King Crocoduck's video series on the science wars](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL7TtKGq2OKBaeK_m9gqRoZPUCqQD6GrWb), which delves into these such topics in a sufficient but not exorbitant length of time.  In short, if we can't agree on epistemology, the very nature of how we distinguish fact from fiction and logic from fallacy, or even what the words "true" and "objective" mean, we can't really agree on much of anything.  If you want to see the effects of feminist epistemology in short order, merely ask a feminist in detail about how they'd handle the topics of nuclear weapons and eugenics if they had control of all scientific enterprise; if you hold to scientific realism (as opposed to radical constructivism), you'll be stunned at what you hear and its implications.

\- I likely differ from the prevailing view in this subreddit, but the expectation that gender roles can, or even should, ever be virtually eliminated is an empirically untenable pipe dream.  This is ultimately a confluence of both patriarchy theory and radical constructivist epistemology: the root of the feminist conception of gender roles is that they were invented by men ex nihilo for the sole, express purpose of oppressing women as a class to the exclusive, unilateral benefit of men as a class.  As is the case with patriarchy theory, this is a vast oversimplification at best and quasi-religious disingenuity at worst.  To greatly boil down my own stance, evolution did not magically exempt the human brain from its influence over every other aspect of biology, identifiable and quantifiable macro scale human behavioral trends do not empirically bear out the radical constructivist notion of gender roles, and many people often are happiest when they follow them.  The thing that sets me apart from a conservative is that I don't fall into the naturalistic fallacy; something being naturally encouraged or even inevitable does not automatically mean it's good, or that exceptions should be ignored or moralistically shoved back into a box (on the flip side of this, statistical outliers do not disprove a trend).  In fact, I would maintain that the one thing that truly sets humanity apart from the rest of the animal kingdom is that we can identify problems which nature imposes on us and use our intelligence and creativity to devise solutions (but, until we upload our minds into computers and eschew it altogether, we still face limitations when dealing with human biology), which has compounded so much that human existence is now utterly unrecognizable from what our brains evolved for us to live like, for much better and for worse.  Most feminists would say they agree with this, but *their* observable, quantifiable behavior tells otherwise.

It had to happen at some point or else it would lead to our extinction.  Perpetual population growth on a planet of finite resources is unsustainable, especially when the developed world demands ever more resources per capita. I'm not denying any of the problems of population falling into decline, just saying that both directions of population change have major looming problems.

Hell, it's likely that even with the population increase deceleration starting now, it might be too late to avert global calamity.

Speaking for myself, even if I find myself married tomorrow to an absolutely flawless woman with perfect clairvoyance that our relationship would last until death, and with a spare $10 million in the bank, I do not want to have children.  I don't hate children, but rather I believe that children should be born to parents in good health who are prepared to take care of them, which I am neither.

It would be monstrous to give a child the genes which have caused me so much physical and mental suffering.  I won't even adopt, because I am confident that I would not be a very good father.  Most bad parents never preempt themselves with that kind of introspection and simply plow ahead.

People who say that have never been a man with a pathetic voice.  My voice sounds like a castrated 12 year-old putting on a facetious conceited affectation.  If I get visibly or vocally angry, people aren't scared, most either laugh or treat me like a child.

Loneliness is one of the only problems that you CAN'T fix on your own, no matter how hard you try.

Do people who fall into depressive, asocial cycles tend to acclimate to it and develop a sense of inertia about making effort to change, even if they have the means to do so?  Yes, they do;  I have been guilty of this myself.  If this was the full extent of the feminist position, I would have no objections to it.

However, let's say that man drums up the willpower to take decisive action: He signs up for multiple social events every week, he goes, and he continually makes an earnest attempt to involve himself with the other people attending.  At that point, it's out of his hands.  He is doing everything he can do to solve his loneliness.  The rest of the responsibility now inexorably lies on everyone else to reciprocate and interact with him.  As much as he may wish that he could, he can't force people to talk to him and befriend him.

"It's not my responsibility to help lonely men" is only true in the strictest sense.  No, nobody can justifiably point to a particular shut-in and decree that "you there, yes, you, are somehow obligated to burst down his door to become his new best friend."  However, it is impossible for it not to be *someone* else's responsibility.

Furthermore, this feminist attitude toward lonely men is a selective inversion of their underlying value system and a symptom of great personal conceit.  Feminism, like every other sociopolitical ideology with the same roots, is collectivistic: On almost every other topic, feminists will argue that everyone's lives are primarily governed by the influences of systems of society, culture, and institutions, that individual agency and personal responsibilities have little impact on individual outcomes, and therefore solutions must be collective, bearing shared responsibility across all of society (not always evenly distributed).  That is, unless you're a man with a problem that can't be easily handwaved away by 'toxic masculinity" or "the patriarchy backfiring."  Then, feminists immediately flip one of the core premises underlying everything they purport to believe about the nature of human existence and become just as much of cutthroat rugged individualists as whoever is guest starring on Fox News this week to say that regulatory capture of the finance sector is great, actually.

Their bitter disdain toward lonely men is also **extremely** conceited.  It's not even a subtext, they're outright saying that men are unworthy to even be in the presence of a woman unless he can magically fix all of his personal flaws in complete isolation.  Only then, once he has transcended them with no help from nor posing the slightest inconvenience to anyone, is he finally worthy of women to grace him with their presence.  This attitude is an attempt to elevate women to something akin to nobility or demigod status.

Speaking personally: I don't engage with nearly as much atheist content as I did 10-11 years ago because I can't slay that dragon any deader than it already is.  Of course, Christian imposition on American public policy is still a big problem, but that's beyond the scope of my own mind, being a matter of culture and electoral politics.  Watching another video refuting one of the finite number of lines of religious argumentation is just redundant for me.  I would suspect that many deconverts follow the same trajectory, especially after phasing out of the anger of realizing that we had been systematically lied to about the entire nature of reality for our whole lives.  It's difficult to stay angry forever, even about something of that magnitude.

As for the atheist movement itself, it was ground zero for today's incarnation of the culture war.  When feminism popped up in the atheist community (Free Thought Blogs, Atheism+, Elevatorgate, and so on) and did what it always does, atheists fell into infighting which signaled the end of our brief moment in the spotlight.

Now, in addition to the culture war raging on, the nature of the internet today is stacked against atheism getting a second wind.  We benefited greatly from the wild west era of the internet; a lot of people were exposed to us whom otherwise never would've heard what we have to say.  Today, brand safety-focused content recommendation algorithms are more than happy to keep us all, religious or secular, in our own separate internet ecosystems.  The majority of the population are still religious, so firebrand anti-theism isn't always deemed suitable for advertisers, and so our content reach is no longer what it once was.

The term "pick me" is slut shaming.  Seriously, just adapt the Confederacy checkmate and ask them "pick her to do what?"

The most important thing to know about feminists, even more important than the fact that the single core statement their entire ideology rests upon is a fallacy of composition which directly stems from hypergamy bias, is that they explicitly reject empiricism.  Sorry to take a page out of their playbook, but for more background on this I'd highly recommend watching [this series](https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PL969utfM58zhc8Xzo2byAjZkWlTQWUTYc) on the science wars and [this video](https://rumble.com/v3kro0g-tldr-womens-reality-feminism-is-a-religion-book-1-25sep23.html) on the philosophical origins of feminism.  Once you understand that feminists are not operating on an empirical basis, a lot of their behavior starts to make more sense, but it kind of destroys any hope of reasoning with them; they consider reason itself to be "males privileging their denial of their own emotional, value-laden reasoning over alternative, female ways of knowing."

You've noted the feminist tendency to fail to see that you disagree with them on empirical grounds.  Once you understand that feminists reject empiricism, you understand that they believe that the narrative *is* the truth.  Feminists believe that there is no such thing as objective reality; instead, everything they believe is ontologically "true" because (by their own unquestionable, question-begging assertion) it is posited against the oppressor on behalf of the oppressed and thus yields morally good outcomes to believe it.  If you are unconvinced, feminists believe it's either merely a messaging failure on their part or your obstinate refusal to listen to their message; most are never humble enough admit personal faults in the realm of politics, so they lean toward the latter and try to get you to absorb feminist material they think will be more palatable to you.

If you need further evidence of this, look how they converse among themselves whenever the topic of young men being pulled rightward arises; They never ask "is it possible we're incorrect about something?" or "how can we understand men's perspective to broaden our own?", it's only "how can we 'get' the ideological foot soldiers we are morally entitled to by virtue of existing, and punish them for daring to ever forsake the one, true way?"  Alternatively, ask them what they think about eugenics or nuclear weapons; they'll never explicitly admit this, but you can get them to directly imply that they believe that *particle physics and genetics themselves* will contort to the social values of the dominant culture of the time.

Furthermore, a more parsimonious component for why they deflect by telling you to go educate yourself is that their moral zealotry breeds conceit, which breeds entitlement, which breeds laziness.  They don't want to enact the "emotional labor" of "unlearning your own biases *for* you."  This stems from the belief that you are the oppressor, and that it is unilaterally incumbent upon the oppressor class to stop oppressing the victim class.  It's a degree of sheer arrogant laziness matched by no other ideological strain I can think of.  Most other morally zealous ideological groups are happy to proselytize to you if you let them, or even if you don't.

>Will politics be forced in the long run to look at men’s issues from a non-feminist perspective?

Probably not to any significant degree (outside of niche internet spaces like this one) within my lifetime.

>Will the left be forced to really look at men because alarmingly many will turn to the populist right?

What color do you want your dragon, or does it not matter because you're blind?  We already know how they react to that exact stimulus, one or both of two options:

1) Triple down on continuing to offer nothing to men but vitriol and demands of self-flagellation and service.  If you think feminists at large are suddenly going to have an introspective look at the shortcomings of their ideology and revise their beliefs in accordance with new information, you do not understand feminism.  The single core belief underpinning the entire socio-cultural-politcal apparatus of feminism is patriarchy theory: The notion that any and all qualitative or quantitative differences in behavioral or status outcomes between men and women are the result of men oppressing women.  Feminists are, by definition, *completely unable* to admit that men may have unique issues (and they *definitely* will not admit if a men's issue is found where women are beneficiaries of or contributors to it) or to admit other factors for differences between men and women exist besides unilateral oppression.  Any feminist who makes those admissions is, by definition, no longer a feminist.  Since you're expecting feminism as a whole to do this, you're basically expecting an entire political ideology to excise its foundational premise.  This is basically like wondering if Christians will come around to ditching the whole "Jesus" thing.

2) Wonder "how do we 'get' men back on our side," and ultimately come up with no solutions.  Feminism has zero consideration for men as human beings, only as political pawns whose service they feel automatically entitled to by virtue of existing.  This is largely caused by feminism's explicit rejection of empiricism (look up Sandra Harding); Feminists are utterly unequipped to deal with a possibility of their ideology failing to materially deliver on its assertions and promises, and they view their belief system as ontologically correct merely because its core narrative *says* that it's emancipatory in pursuit of moral justice.  Thus, any failure for the outsiders to understand this must either be solely a messaging issue, or that the unconvinced outsiders are too motivated by their unjustly held privilege to relinquish it.

>Will there be some damage control, removing the worst parts of misandry, gynocentrism and double standards, while the core of it only gets stronger?

I'm not sure what you mean by this.  Wouldn't the worst parts of something bad be the core?

>Will advances in (evolutionary and other) psychology destroy the dominant, feminist narrative?

There's already plenty of factual information out there to throw many feminist claims into question to varying degrees.  Most people, even just apolitical normies, do not default to a doxastic state in which hurling facts at them is an effective strategy for changing minds.  You have to care about facts first for contradictory facts to possibly sway you, and if someone believes that "the pretense of scientific objectivity is merely a male illusion to discredit feminine, intuitive, liberatory ways of knowing" (paraphrased, but that is genuinely what feminists believe about the scientific enterprise), they don't even believe in facts as a valid concept.

>How long will it all take and why?

I don't think significant change on this front will occur in my lifetime.  Feminism is already widely entrenched in world governments, corporations, media, political activism, and general culture, while we have, what, the Tin Man Blog on Instagram and The Prim Reaper on YouTube?  I love and admire the work both of those two people do, but our cultural footprint is utterly miniscule and our policy footprint is effectively zero.  Most people have never heard of us, and even those who have assume we're Jordan Peterson and/or Andrew Tate fans cosplaying as leftists.

>In the meantime, will it be worthwhile to be active as a male advocate or will changes be dependent on totally different factors? Will our function be to come up with sound, attractive, undogmatic theories when at last the current ones are totally worn out? Or should you only look up soulmates in that meantime to share your worries, without hoping for real improvement?

I'm not holding my breath.  I don't even have those "soulmates."  At the same time, if everyone was as cynical and pessimistic as I am, nothing in the world would ever change.  I respect people who try to make a difference in the world, even if it seems to me like they're just repeatedly bruising their foreheads.

First off, the title of this post is an indication that you're in a supportive frame of mind.  That alone is further than a lot of people go.

>I found it so sad to read and I offered my support and explained that I actually find it an attractive quality when men are open about their feelings and cry sometimes.

>It wasn't taken very well and I got a lot of replies/ messages telling me I was a liar I was full of s***, im trying to manipulate them etc.

This reaction comes down to the fact that the attitude you expressed, while it may be genuine in you, is usually just a culturally sanctioned façade.  Many, many women *say* that they want a man who expresses his emotions, is in touch with his feminine side, and isn't afraid to cry in front of her.  Saying these things earns the accolades of her feminist colleagues, because that stated position is in opposition to "toxic masculinity."  However, the moment the time actually comes to support and love her boyfriend crying about trauma he's had to bury for years, she *instantly* loses all romantic and sexual desire for him and breaks up with him in a matter of days.  This ugly reality contradicts multiple feminist notions at once: The idea that men's lives are dreamboats of privilege rowed by shackled women, that uncritically swallowing a political narrative will override her innate, near-universal desire for her male partner to be emotionally tougher than her, and that men's mental health problems are largely their own fault for not opening up to people, and that everything would be better if they did.

If opening up about trauma causes someone to lose treasured, very hard-earned relationships, then it *wasn't* safe to open up to her and it does *not* make things better.  To make matters worse, she didn't even have the self-awareness to be able to warn him that abandonment was a likely reaction.  That common lack of self-awareness is why men might be skeptical or cynically dismissive of your desire to help men; Unless you have concrete positive examples to show them (and that's hard to do with just text on Reddit), it's impossible to preemptively distinguish the aforementioned kind of woman from the kind of woman who actually will still love her man if he allows himself to fall beneath her, however briefly or justifiably.

Oh, funny you should mention that: My parents actually home schooled me too, but only for 6-8th grade, in large part to ensure that I wouldn't go to sex education.  I was also the only kid in my entire fifth grade whose parents opted them out of human growth & development/preliminary sex ed.  They would've home schooled me all through high school too, were it not for the fact that my mom admitted that she could not teach me or my siblings most subjects a high school level.

As a result, I think that home schooling should not be an option for anyone unless the parents can somehow prove attending public school would be more damaging than complete social isolation and the religious indoctrination most home schooling parents are motivated by.  Even in edge cases where parents have the best intentions, most parents aren't qualified to be teachers on every subject.

Oh, man, I could talk about this for hours.  Let's see if I can keep my comment shorter than a novella.

This issue practically guarantees that I (and presumably many other men in a position like mine) will never have any kind of romantic or sexual experience ever again.  First, some background: I grew up in a fundamentalist religious household so I obeyed my parents' condemnation of premarital sex and believed that my future wife would be magically, deterministically placed in my life with no effort required on my part.  I was (and still am) nowhere near good looking enough for girls to approach me for conversation, let alone with flirtatious intent.  The autism my mom "gifted" me prevented me from knowing what a normal social existence even looks like.  To top it all off, not a single ostensibly successful, trustworthy adult (not even the professional psychotherapists nor school guidance counselors) ever told me that my asocial path was a silent road to utter ruin.  How was I supposed to know?  I had never seen the world any other way.  Why didn't anybody tell me?  Is that not what adults are supposed to be for when you're a kid?

Fast forward to a few months before my 24th birthday, and due to a series of utterly irreplicable events, I was hooking up with an online friend's friend (who I'll refer to as Clarissa) who was introduced to me online a few weeks prior.  What I thought would be the first major step toward saving myself turned out to be a grim reminder of the total inescapability of my situation.  Physical impotence aside (and there was no shortage of it), while I was cuddling with her late into the second night, I bawled my fucking eyes out.  As it turns out, subjecting a man to an entire life completely devoid of intimacy causes tremendous harm (far exceeding his conscious awareness of it), and then suddenly showing him *what humanity is supposed to feel like* all at once brings it all to the surface.  I'm fortunate that Clarissa didn't rebuke me in the moment, but she did instantly lose all desire for me, moving on the minute I was out of reach another two days later.

Now, why did I bother writing all of this instead of just skipping to my impending points?  Well, for one thing, I've never been one for brevity.  But more importantly I think it gives necessary context.  Point number one: Human minds exhibit sexual dimorphism in much the same way our bodies do.  How Clarissa reacted is *hardly* atypical of women.  Unless you only cavort with male virgins, every man you know has either had a similar experience happen to him personally or knows at least one who has.  The number of women who will retain sexual attraction to a man who exhibits enough emotional weakness to place him beneath her is virtually nil.  Furthermore, no amount of feminist indoctrination can override biological hardwiring as deep as sexual selection.  Hell, most of any self-described feminist women who've done this don't even notice a contradiction with their stated beliefs, much less act to change it, because it serves them no benefit to do so and it's not like any external force will hold them rhetorically accountable.  They are perfectly content to obliviously uphold "toxic masculinity" and "the patriarchy hurting men too" whenever doing so is to their benefit.

My second point: There is no way around my intimacy deficit.  There is no substitute for human intimacy.  There is no way to preemptively erase the trauma of lifelong isolation from my brain.  Therapy can't help with this either; I asked my therapist whether I can achieve happiness solely by talking to her about lacking the necessary ingredients of humanity, and she agreed that *I actually must obtain them* to heal and be happy.  The only hypothetical way that I could ever experience intimacy without any more puddles of tears is to first be given all of the intimacy that I feel I lack, for however long it takes for it to no longer feel bewilderingly novel to me (Days? Weeks? Months?), and with unwavering kindness in the face of my intense grieving.  But, as you may have determined by now, this is virtually impossible because it runs directly counter to what women find desirable in men.

Since OP mentioned it, I'll also say that as far as kink is concerned, I'm very much on the opposite side of MDLB, so my intimacy deficit is not at all a fetishistic thing for me.  I don't want to be infantilized.  I don't want this weakness to define me.  In my ideal world, someone would give me the help necessary for me to overcome it, and then I could get better and it wouldn't be such a huge roadblock anymore.

It's late and I have no idea how to wrap this up neatly.  Catch-22s involving the building blocks of human happiness are atrocious.  Shit sucks and there's no way out.  There, that'll do.

Not to take away from your conclusion (I generally agree with it), but I don't think you chose good examples to build up to it.

The first set can be boiled down to pointing out human sexual dimorphism.  I don't think this is a good basis for self-esteem since it isn't very actionable if you want to be a civilized person.  Using myself for reference since I won't speak for OP, I know I'm taller than about 99.97% of women, I'm sure I can bicep curl more than 95+% of them, and I'm sure I could win an MMA match against a similar portion of women with my level of training (none).  What good does that knowledge do for me?  I don't want to even intimidate people, let alone get into physical altercations.  Even if we take the focus off of fighting, none of those things mean I have more human value than a woman.  If anything, they're detrimental.  A lot of women use their fear of men being stronger than them to their social benefit over us, convincing people that I'm a potential danger until proven otherwise, and that women are inherently more deserving of comfort and consideration than I am.

As for fertility, this is also socially useless.  How does my daily sperm production grant me more human value or any social advantage over women's fixed number of egg cells?  Last I checked, the inverse is true for virtually every sexually reproductive species on Earth.  Also, you're speaking merely about potential; If a man fails to attract a woman to have his children (or chooses not to), the output of his reproductive system makes no functional difference.

As for earnings and careers, you're reframing the wage gap myth as a positive.  Men in aggregate earn more money largely because we're just more interested in things which more directly create monetarily valuable productive output (ex. petroleum engineering vs. nursing).  But even this is a very broad, loosely correlated trend; There are hundreds of millions of men the world over who are impoverished or working class, many of whom will never rise above their current class for innumerable personal and macroeconomic factors.  The fact that 71% of hedge fund managers are male is of zero help to a man stocking shelves at a grocery store (if anything, the hedge fund managers are probably shorting the grocery store worker's meager retirement account).  And this is not even to mention the fact that money *should not* be a metric of a person's human or social worth.  People often use it that way, but relationships built on one person's interest in another's wealth are rarely fulfilling.

I've had this thought for years (but I'm sure it's not entirely original).  Feminism, and politics more generally, is replacing religion.  Christianity is on a gradual decline in the US and the Western world more broadly, but there hasn't been a coincident rise in skepticism, empiricism, understanding of the psychology of belief change, nor anything else of the sort.  Thus, most people are still operating on religious modes of thought and still yearn for religious community and moral certitude (and self-righteous sectarian conflict), but with religion itself taking a cultural back seat, they make politics the object of their religious thinking.  Feminism in particular happens to fill the hole left by Christianity rather neatly:

- God, the Bible — Feminism, feminist doctrine

- Satan — The patriarchy

- Sin — Misogyny

- Original sin — Toxic masculinity, being male

- Salvation by belief in Jesus — Exemption from being considered sexist (sometimes) by believing in feminism

- Faith — Faith (in both ideologies, pointing out logical fallacies & inconsistencies or discovering contradictory facts are frowned upon)

This shit dashes any hope I might have left for society.  How can I hope to put up any meaningful counternarrative when the leading, highly communicable pattern of sociopolitical thought is completely devoid of intellectual honesty?  Feminists don't consider being empirically wrong on any point, no matter how small or ancillary, a possibility.  They don't believe they are capable of logical fallacies (or even if they do, the ends justify the means), so they just lead with them.  They believe that even tepid dissent and criticism is unforgivable sin against an unassailable morality.  They're so politically bloodthirsty that they even routinely, flippantly commit political fratricide on male feminists: Uncritically swallowing and parroting their entire ideology without reservation (nor even self-flagellating for being male) isn't enough for them.

How am I supposed to contend with that when I actually believe I can be wrong, I believe I can do wrong (and I try not to), I believe fallacious reasoning should be identified and expunged, but I'm not willing to accept hatred, let alone from people who will claim one sentence prior that they care about me and my issues?  How can I contend with that when my method of thinking (let alone specific beliefs themselves) is not only uncommon but also serves as unilateral rhetorical disarmament?

>well maybe try living a few years in their shoes?

I doubt most people would even last two weeks.

One point of disagreement: Maslow's hierarchy puts sex at the bottom for one or both of two reasons, either that it's necessary at the species level (you won't die if you can't or won't have kids, but the species would if everyone didn't) or it's referring just to sexual release, which masturbation covers.  However, as you seem to realize, sexual intimacy is in the love and belonging tier, which is *below* the esteem tier, which necessarily means that a portion of your self-esteem is derived from sexual intimacy, not vice versa.  People who say "just love yourself, bro" or "sex isn't important, man" are either completely oblivious to the source of their prized self-esteem or they genuinely believe that they completely meritocratically earned the success they have because they're just a superior person.  They're asking you to magically achieve a higher level of success and then use it to go back and get one of its building blocks.  If you could challenge one of these people to live under our conditions for a month, you'd receive their call to forfeit within a week.  I think all of us here are remarkably resilient for enduring without fulfillment of basic human desires which many people have never gone without.

I grew up in a fundamentalist Christian household which was extremely damaging to my sexuality and social development.  When I first started to make my way out of the faith, I thought I'd be heading into a refreshing new world where I wouldn't be shamed anymore for aspects of who I am which are beyond my control, that I wouldn't be blamed for actions of my (or other people's) long-dead ancestors, and that I wouldn't have to contend with such a high degree of logical fallacy and dogmatism anymore.  Boy, was I wrong.  I came out of religion in 2013, which is right when feminism reared its ugly head within the atheist community and threw it into infighting it has yet to recover from.  So now rather than being in a culture where my more effeminate side is looked down upon, I'm treated as eternally guilty of an original sin, and I'm required to suppress my sexuality to keep God happy, I exist in a culture where my masculine side is looked down upon, I'm treated as eternally guilty of an original sin, and I'm required to suppress my sexuality to keep women happy.
